1: Feature engineering and feature selection. Lectures twenty five and twenty six, with Doctor Shital Bhatt at Vidyashilp University.
2: Today's roadmap has two parts. Part one: build better features, with feature construction, interaction terms, polynomial features, and the curse of dimensionality. Part two: keep only useful features, with why select features, filter methods, wrapper methods, embedded methods, and a comparison of the three. The running example is Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention: twelve thousand three hundred thirty website sessions, with the target Revenue, did the visitor buy?
3: Same model, better features, better result. On the Online Shoppers data, a logistic regression on the ten original features gets a test R O C A U C of point eight five five. Adding eight constructed features lifts it to point eight nine eight. Adding three interaction terms lifts it to point nine oh four. That is plus point oh five of R O C A U C without changing the model, only the features. Better data beats a fancier algorithm.
4: Feature construction: new columns from old. You combine existing columns using domain knowledge to make a column that says the pattern more directly. It is like cooking: the raw ingredients are already there, and the recipe makes them useful. The model does not have to discover the pattern by itself. Example, one website session: three administrative pages, zero informational pages, seventeen product pages, and six hundred seconds in total. Constructed features: total pages equals three plus zero plus seventeen, twenty. Average time per page equals six hundred divided by twenty, thirty seconds. Product share equals seventeen over twenty, point eight five.
5: Five recipes for constructing features. One, total: add related columns, like total pages equals admin plus info plus product. Two, ratio: divide to remove a size effect, like average time per page equals duration divided by pages. Three, flag: turn a condition into one or zero, like has page value equals page values greater than zero. Four, log: shrink a long right tail, like log of one plus page values, where skew falls from six point four to one point eight. Five, band: cut a number into groups, like session short, medium, long or very long.
6: Example: one flag splits buyers from browsers. Has page value equals one if the visitor saw a page that has a value, for example a product before checkout. When the flag is zero, the purchase rate is three point nine percent. When it is one, the purchase rate is fifty six point three percent, fourteen times higher. One line of code, and it becomes one of the two strongest features in the data.
7: Example: bands show a step like effect. Pandas qcut cuts total duration into four groups with the same number of sessions. The purchase rate by band is four point three percent for short, twelve point six for medium, twenty one for long, and twenty four for very long. The rate rises from four to twenty four percent, then flattens. Longer is better, but only up to a point. A band lets even a simple model capture that flattening.
8: Good practice for constructing features. One, start from domain knowledge. Ask what an expert would look at. In shopping: effort, value, intent and season. Two, never use the target. A feature built from revenue, or from future data, is leakage: perfect in the lab and useless in real use. Three, guard divisions. Ratios divide by zero for empty sessions, so replace zero with missing, then fill with zero. Four, test every new feature: same model, same split, before versus after. Weak features become candidates for removal.
9: Interaction: the effect of A depends on B. Fertiliser helps a crop a lot, but only if there is water. A discount sells more, but much more during the festive season. A linear model adds effects, it cannot multiply them on its own. Without interaction, y equals b zero plus b one A plus b two B. With interaction, y equals b zero plus b one A plus b two B plus b three times A times B. So we give it the product A times B as a new column. If b three is not zero, the slope of A changes with B.
10: Detect an interaction with a two way table: purchase rate by visitor type and page value. Page value lifts new visitors from six point nine percent to eighty six point four percent. But it lifts returning visitors only from three point three to fifty one point two percent. Unequal jumps mean an interaction. The new feature is page value times is returning. After adding three interaction terms, the A U C went from point eight nine eight to point nine oh four.
11: Polynomial features: squares and products. They add powers, x squared, x cubed, and all cross products of the chosen columns. This lets a straight line model fit curves and interactions. In Python, use Polynomial Features with degree equals two. For inputs a and b at degree two, the new columns are a squared, a times b, and b squared, beside the originals. With real data, three inputs, page values, exit rates and product related, give nine columns: the three originals, their three squares, and their three pairwise products.
12: Columns explode as the degree rises. The number of columns equals the combinations of n plus d choose d, minus one, where n is the number of inputs and d the degree. For three inputs at degrees one to five: three, nine, nineteen, thirty four and fifty five columns. For ten inputs: ten, sixty five, two eighty five, one thousand, and three thousand two. And from our eighty five encoded features, degree three gives one hundred nine thousand seven hundred thirty five columns, for only twelve thousand three hundred thirty rows.
13: Using polynomial features safely. One, scale first: x squared of a large number becomes huge, so standardise before or after the expansion so all columns are comparable. Two, keep the degree low: degree two is usually enough, and degree three or more mostly adds noise and over fits. Three, pair with selection: expand a few chosen columns, then use regularisation or feature selection to keep what helps. All three fit in one pipeline: polynomial features of degree two, standard scaler, and an L one penalised logistic regression with C equals point oh five.
14: The curse of dimensionality. Finding a friend on a one hundred metre road is easy. On a one hundred by one hundred metre field it is harder. In a one hundred metre cube building it is very hard. Every new feature is a new direction to search. With real data, we cut each feature into four bins, giving four to the d cells. The chart shows the percentage of cells containing any of the twelve thousand three hundred thirty sessions. With one feature, one hundred percent; with two, seventy five; with four, forty four; with six, eight point two; with eight, two; and with ten features only point two percent.
15: Three symptoms of too many features. One, sparse data: with ten features, only point two percent of the space has data, about five sessions per occupied cell. The same twelve thousand three hundred thirty sessions are spread ever thinner. Two, distances lose meaning: in many dimensions the nearest and farthest points are almost equally far, so K N N and clustering suffer. Three, over fitting: with many columns and few rows, the model memorises noise, giving a high train score and a low test score. Test A U C is point seven four three at two hundred eighty five columns, compared with point eight seven eight at ten.
16: Evidence: more columns, worse test score. We train logistic regression on four hundred sessions. With degree one, ten columns, the train A U C is high and the test A U C is point eight seven eight. With degree two, sixty five columns, the test score is lower. With degree three, two hundred eighty five columns, the train score climbs to point nine nine six, the model fits its four hundred rows almost perfectly, but the test score falls to point seven four three. It has memorised noise. The extra two hundred seventy five columns hurt, not help.
17: How to beat the curse. One, more data, meaning more rows per region of the space. Two, feature selection: keep only the useful columns, which is next. Three, regularisation: penalise large coefficients, L one or L two. Four, dimensionality reduction: P C A and friends combine columns. Five, domain knowledge: build few, meaningful features. A rule of thumb for a classifier: aim for at least about ten cases of the rarer class per feature. For Pima diabetes, with two sixty eight positives, that means about twenty seven features at most.
18: Feature selection: three families. The goal is a smaller set of columns that predicts as well: simpler, faster, less over fitting, and easier to explain. Filter: score each feature before the model, with a statistic, keep the top k, then train the model. Wrapper: search around the model. Try a subset, train the model, score it, and repeat for many subsets to find the best subset. Embedded: selection inside the model. Train a model with a penalty or importance, and it outputs the selected features.
19: Filter methods score each feature on its own. Variance threshold works on any feature with no target, and keeps features that are not almost constant. Pearson correlation works on numeric features and a numeric or zero one target, and keeps features with large absolute r. The A N O V A F test works on numeric features with a categorical target, and keeps features with very different class means. The chi square test works on categorical or count features, and keeps features that are not independent of the target. Mutual information works on any type, and keeps features that reduce uncertainty about the target. Filters are very fast and model free, a good first screen, but they ignore interactions and keep near duplicates. Caution: variance depends on scale, so tiny valued columns, like rates from zero to point two, look constant even when useful.
20: Filter example: the A N O V A F score, top eight. Log page values scores six thousand six hundred seventy two, has page value five thousand five thirty nine, page values three thousand one fifty four, page value times returning nineteen sixty four, page value times Q four twelve eighty five, exit rates four forty three, total pages two sixty eight, and product related two forty nine. Five of the top five are versions of the same signal: page value. A filter scores each feature alone, so it happily keeps all five. And month November never makes the list, though models find it useful.
21: Wrapper methods let the model choose. Forward selection starts empty, adds the one feature that improves the score most, and repeats until k features. Backward elimination starts with all, removes the feature whose loss hurts least, and repeats until k features. R F E, recursive feature elimination, fits the model, drops the feature with the smallest weight, refits, and repeats. The strength: wrappers see interactions and redundancy, and usually find the best small subset. The weakness: they are slow, training the model hundreds of times, and can over fit the selection.
22: Embedded methods select while training. First, the L one, or Lasso, penalty: it pushes weak coefficients to exactly zero. A smaller C, a stronger penalty, means fewer features. The chart shows the largest non zero L one coefficients, twenty of eighty five kept: log page values point seven seven, has page value point six nine, month November point three four, visitor type new point one two, administrative minus point one three, and exit rates minus point three two. Second, tree importance: random forests record how much each feature splits the data well, and you keep the top ones.
23: Filter versus wrapper versus embedded. Does it use a model? Filter, no, just a statistic. Wrapper, yes, trains many times. Embedded, yes, trains once. Speed: filter is fastest, wrapper slowest, embedded medium. Seeing interactions and redundancy: filter no, wrapper yes, embedded partly. Main risk: filter keeps duplicates, wrapper over fits the selection, embedded is tied to one model type. Typical use: filter as a first screen of many features, wrapper to fine tune a short list, embedded as the everyday default. Examples: correlation, A N O V A and mutual information; forward, backward and R F E; Lasso and tree importance.
24: A practical selection workflow in four steps. One, clean: drop constant and duplicate columns. Two, screen: use a filter to make a shortlist, with correlation or mutual information. Three, choose: use embedded L one or a wrapper on the shortlist. Four, check: score on unseen test rows. And the golden rule: select features using the training rows only. If the test rows help choose the features, the test score is no longer honest. That is data leakage.
25: Key takeaways. Construct and interact: build features that state the pattern directly, and test each one. Polynomial features grow as n plus d choose d minus one, so use low degree, scale, then select. Too many columns give a sparse space, weak distances and over fitting. And remember: filter is a fast screen, wrapper gives the best small set, and embedded is the everyday default.
